Messages.Author: Guy Keen
Messages.Body:
With the April 95 FAQ release it seems apparent to me that some
card/rule issues still haven't been clarified. In particuar, I'm
thinking of cards like Fame, Rotschreck, and Charming Lobby. After all
the discussion that has taken place on the net regarding these
and othercards/rules, we should be able to reach playable
inerpretations acceptable to the majority of players.

This is not to level criticism at the design team (some contributors to
this newsgroup would do well to remember that no-one or one group holds
all the right answers), because most of the rulings in the current
release are fine. But, IMO, a few of them still don't work, and that's
what needs to be fixed.

My idea: that a small group (say 3?) of dedicated and experienced Jyhad
"Elders" be elected or chosen. I'm particularly thinking of people like
Alan, Curt, James et al. Periodically, they would open threads on this
group for OFFICIAL discussion, with a view to ultimately producing a
ruling, interpretation or decision (like fix the card text) for
OFFICIAL submission to Tom Wylie or the design team.

Provided that the WOTC reps are receptive and reasonable about this srt
of assistance I can only see positive benefits as an outcome. There's
no way Tom or whoever else can monitor all the net discussions on their
own, and this seems like a good way of keeping them aware of current
opinions and ideas. WOTC need this sort of input to keep this brilliant
game on an even keel. And I think a lot more can be gained by helping
them rather than heaping scorn.

Tom;

When the same thing can be said in many different ways, each of which
causes a different emotional reaction in the listener/reader, this is
defined as semantics.

Saying 'Just because' has negative semantic connotations to many people.
It indicates that you (personally) know and aren't going to tell us; that
it is that way because you (proxy for DT) are in power and have made that
decision and we aren't important enough to know the answer; that there
_isn;t_ a better answer but you can't let anyone know that because that
would weaken your position.

Nobody likes to be made to feel unimportant and/or insignificant; the
answer 'Just Because' has those connotations for many because that is the
kind of answer they were given when they were on the young end of a
parent/child relationship. As adults, people feel they deserve better and
resent feeling like they are being treated like children.

If you really don't know, as you say and I believe, then the best answer
is a simple, "I don't know. I wasn't told either." This is the truth and
alienates no one; indeed - it even brings them to your side as they now
feel a kinship of ignorance with you.

If you do know but cannot say for whatever reason, then say so; "I am not
allowed to tell you - I have been forbidden." People will then
understand that you are not in control of the answer you can give in that
situation and not blame you personally.

If you _do_ know but the answer is too long for you to go through the
whole thing, say that too; "I do not have time/desire to go into full
details; many of the suggestions you have come up with were tried and
rejected for one reason or another." Most people will respect that time
is a significant consideration when answering as many posts as you do, and
will appreciate knowing that their viewpoint was at least considered
before the final way was chosen, or that maybe they have come up with
something no one has thought of before.

Giving a flip, casual answer to a serious questioncan have negative
repercussions; in this case, the phrase 'Just Because' implies an '...I
say so' at the end to many people. It only serves to make people hostile
and alienate them. Semantics is a powerful thing, and can manipulate
people in many ways - often inintentionally or unknowingly. The truth is
usually the best answer; you treat people like adults and not children,
and let them know exactly where you (personally) stand, which for most
will build the level of respect and not weaken it.

Believe me; most people would rather respect someone than scorn them, if
given the chance.

obey our will" to "these liasison aren't proving to be too effective" and
"the Fame ruling seems to have been made in ignorance of a couple of months
net discussion" as you seem to be doing. Does it occur to you that they may
be perfectly well aware of your opinions and just don't _agree_ with them?

First of all, this is not a democracy here. A bunch of people on this
particular board coming to consensus on something is not and should not be
the necessary and sufficient reason for the DT to act on something. The
design team may have any number of considerations in doing what they do that
you may or may not be aware of. On the bottom line, these guys are responsible
for the rules of a game that puts food in their mouths. They'll do what they
do for those reasons - not because you guys happen to think something in the
game is not right. If the two considerations correspond as we might hope they
often do, fine. But when they don't, what you want loses.

Also, keep in mind that people here are only a narrow cross-section of their
potential customers. There's other feedback they have to consider and some of
it might be running counter to the consensus that comes up here. This is only
one data point in the picture.

So don't say the existing liaisons on the net aren't working. That may be
true or it may not - only the WotC personel involved could evaluate that
accurately. Perhaps it's not producing the results you'd hoped for. But is
that because it's failing or because your expectations are too high?

Frederick Scott (fre...@anthrax.cisco.com) wrote:

: I think your making an error here in going from (essentially) "they didn't
: obey our will" to "these liasison aren't proving to be too effective"

When many people who have spent innumerable hours playing the game,
thinking about the game's theory of design (without being privy to the
_actual_ design theories) and discussing the mechanics of the game can
all come to a general consensus on something that is broken within the
context of the game, this is a good indication (at least) that it may
actually be broken.

When these same people are customers of that game, (thus partially
responsible for the game even surviving), and have taken great pains to
introduce others to that game and answer any questions that a new player
might have, then it can be seen that these people are truly interested in
the survival of that game.

When these people are then told by the people representing the company
that produces the game that their input has little or no value, and their
ideas are misguided at best and a waste of time at worst, then I would
say that the company is not effectively listening to the people.

: "the Fame ruling seems to have been made in ignorance of a couple of months
: net discussion" as you seem to be doing. Does it occur to you that they may

: be perfectly well aware of your opinions and just don't _agree_ with them?

Yes, it does. Tom has mentioned that he cannot/will not continually
re-post the same statements detailing why a certain decision was made and
others were ignored. I believe that were he to post it _once_, enough
people would read it and archive it that any future questions along the
same line could be answered by a synopsis or re-posting of the original
post. This would _save_ Tom time in the long run, (IMHO) and would have
the side-effect of many more well-informed players. Perhaps WotC wants to
avoid that side-effect, however, and prefers to keep people in the dark
about rationale, feeding them only rules.

: First of all, this is not a democracy here.

Correct. It is a dictatorship, with the DT as its head. Pardon us if
some of us chafe under its shackles and prefer to think for ourselves.

: A bunch of people on this

: particular board coming to consensus on something is not and should not be
: the necessary and sufficient reason for the DT to act on something.

Correct, but it is at least an indication that this area should be given
some serious consideration - especially when the people who came to
consensus probably spend a greater total percentage of their time
discussing Jyhad than the DT does.

: The

: design team may have any number of considerations in doing what they do that
: you may or may not be aware of.

One of our constant cries is, "Make us aware of these considerations!"

: On the bottom line, these guys are responsible

: for the rules of a game that puts food in their mouths. They'll do what they
: do for those reasons - not because you guys happen to think something in the
: game is not right. If the two considerations correspond as we might hope they
: often do, fine. But when they don't, what you want loses.

Correct. We do not do this for food - we do this for enjoyment and
relaxation. The fact that these people who _do_ do this sort of thing
for food have a huge resource available to make their jobs easier and the
game 'better/more successful' and _choose not to use it_ (TTBOMK) is what
frustrates us. (me, anyway.)

: Also, keep in mind that people here are only a narrow cross-section of their
: potential customers.

What, people who play Jyhad and own a computer? People who play Jyhad
and have a little extra spare time on their hands to read a newsgroup
about it? Neither of these would seem to be a limiting factor in getting
a broad cross-range of types of people whjo play Jyhad; it's not like
this is the Aryan Brotherhood of Jyhad Players or anything...

: There's other feedback they have to consider and some of

: it might be running counter to the consensus that comes up here.

They have _other_ groups on tap that do little else but sit around and
discuss Jyhad Game Theory and Design?

: This is only

: one data point in the picture.

Correction: _I_ am only one data point. _Curt_ is only one data point.
_Scott_ is only one data point... together, we all make up a large
cross-section of players representing many different views on how the
game should be played. When all these people can _agree_ on something...

: So don't say the existing liaisons on the net aren't working.

They aren't working _for me_ (or for Curt, I'd gather), and that is the
only yardstick I can measure by. If I put a dollar in a coke machine and
nothing comes out, I assume it didn't work, or that maybe my dollar was
faulty. If many people cannot get the machine to work, then it is the
assumption that the machine is faulty, not the users.

: That may be

: true or it may not - only the WotC personel involved could evaluate that
: accurately. Perhaps it's not producing the results you'd hoped for.

True - we would like reasoned thought and a few explanations. Sometimes
we get one, sometimes the other.

: But is

: that because it's failing or because your expectations are too high?

I have generally seen it echoed that Jyhad is believed to be the most
complex, most balanced, all-around best CCG on the market. Is it too
much to expect that the makers will continue to treat it that way, or to
assume tha the people playing it might actually have relevant or valuable
input on the game?

response from a WotC representative through your propragando-matic interpreter

an accurate one.

I think the trouble here is that you've got some idea in your head that
what's decided here ought to go straight to top of the agenda at the next
design team weekly meeting. Furthermore, you no doubt think that the response
from the design team ought to be forthcoming later that day - if not total
submission to your will, then a well-reasoned and eloquently written statement

course.

That's not going to happen. While I'm sure that the design team is
undoubtably sensitive to extremely unpopular aspects of the game, there is

conspiring to take over the dictatorship and put yourselves in charge.

>

a thing as "an indication that this area should be given some serious
consideration" is not something that will yield a visible result. They may
very well have taken that indication but nothing has happened that yielded
the result you wanted - how would you know?

You would only know if they made a visible alteration - which I think is
what you're _really_ demanding here. Basically, you don't just want them
take it as indication that this are should be given some serious consideration,
you want them to: 1) accept your opinion on the matter; and 2) DO SOMETHING.
And that's not so reasonable, IMHO.

>: that you may or may not be aware of.
>
>One of our constant cries is, "Make us aware of these considerations!"

likely to be highly unpopular. But I don't think it's very practical for
them to document the precise reasoning for absolutely everything they do.
And some considerations may be difficult to understand by players as
opposed to game designers, who are often likely to get blasted from some
direction or other no matter _what_ they do - or don't do.

>game 'better/more successful' and _choose not to use it_ (TTBOMK) is what
>frustrates us. (me, anyway.)

You have no idea to what extent they choose to use it. All you know is how
often a concern expressed here seems to be addressed by WotC. Unfortunately,
this by itself doesn't really give us an indication of how much we're
listened to. It depends on who else they listen to and how their decisions
have to be made.

>: Also, keep in mind that people here are only a narrow cross-section of their
>: potential customers.
>
>What, people who play Jyhad and own a computer? People who play Jyhad
>and have a little extra spare time on their hands to read a newsgroup
>about it? Neither of these would seem to be a limiting factor in getting
>a broad cross-range of types of people whjo play Jyhad; it's not like

Yes, people who own a computer and have a little (_little_?!? sheesh!)
extra spare time on their hands to read a newsgroup. This is a very
small and very specialized population. So small that out of all the
people I know who play Magic (and I know quite a few), I know only two or
three people who read the r.g.t-c.magic groups and no one else who posts.
And at that, it isn't even they only group of such people.

>: There's other feedback they have to consider and some of

>

and design is not the only qualification for being a source of input.
Anyone who might buy this product is someone who's opinion they might want
to listen to.

>
>Correction: _I_ am only one data point. _Curt_ is only one data point.
>_Scott_ is only one data point... together, we all make up a large
>cross-section of players representing many different views on how the

they see as problems. However, it should be understood that it is never
guaranteed that these suggestions will be adopted, that the design team
is not necessarily going to agree that the "problem" in question is something
that needs fixing, and that we are typically reluctant to release actual
changes to the rules midstream. Plugging holes is one thing, but official
rules changes are best left to be incorporated when new editions come out.

Mr F. Scott,

Could you answer me a few questions (if you could please indulge such an insignificant
sub-unit of a data point as myself)???

What position or proximity to the design team do you hold that you have such a detailed
knowledge of their motives and of individuals within WOTC's reasons for making specific
rulings and decisions. You seem to know Tom Wylie's reasons for saying the fateful "just
because" better than he does. If you're perfectly happy with the rulings that have come
out from the design team, then explain to me the logic behind their series of rulings on
Rotschreck, as one instance.

How long have you been playing Jyhad and how often do you play? This is important. I've
been playing many times a week for 6 months and I still have many questions and queries.
I won't claim to be an expert on anything. But there's my vested interest. I love the
game, and love playing it. So why do you think I offer a suggestion for the possible
submission of official rulings? Simply to try to help make things better.

There are no-doubt hundreds of other Jyhad players on the net who have been playing
longer and more often than myself. These people are of all ages, from numerous other
countries. I'm Australian for example, and I've been playing extensively in England. If
you consider that a forum that focuses discussion from such people that read this group
is so insignificant and trifling that we should not be surprised if the design team
ignores us altogether, then I really wonder where you're coming from. What is your
relationship to Jyhad?

If there's another single group of Jyhad players that is bigger, from a broader
demographic cross-section, with more experience than the readers of this group, point
them out to me, and tell me what attention WOTC pays to them. And all this stems from the
seemingly misguided notion that some of us think we might be able to offer something
useful to WOTC, and we'd really like to help. That's where I'm coming from anyway.

I'd really like to get some feedback from DT/WOTC rep on my original thread. Because if
genuine efforts to do something positive/constructive/pro-active to keep this game
working are going to be met with either silence or big negative responses like Mr
Scott's, then I'm wasting my time.

Not quite. When dealing with language, it is possible to be quite
precise about exactly what one means when writing, and it is equally
possible for someone reading that written message to determine exactly
what is said. While I can never go inside the DT/Richard Garfield's head
and know what they _meant_ to say, I can sure as heck analyse what they
_did_ say and understand that.

Example: Rotschreck. The card is quite clear in what it _says_ if one
takes a literal and semantic reading of it, but that is apparently not
what the designers _meant_ to say, as evidenced by the rules fixes.

the card; I _will_ listen if you tell me that what was printed wasn't the
way the card was meant to work and give me a few reasons behind that
statement.

The same sort of thing applies to logic. One person's logic may be open
to interpretation, but when many people with similar knowledge or better
read the same information and come up with the same conclusions, then the
logic has withstood scrutiny and is that much closer to being called sound.

however: "When E.F.Hutton speaks, everybody listens," for example. Tom
used to be nothing more than a guy who gave his opinions on Magic rules
and rulings, and people respected them because they showed evidence of
sound logic and much forethought. I still respect what he says about how
Magic works, because I know that he has spent many, _many_ more hours
thinking about that game than have I. Ditto with the DT, to some extent.

do the opinions of frequent posters to this group, i.e. Curt, Scott, Joe,
James, et al., as they [Tom/DT] do not show the same level of rules
knowledge and thought as do the people I mentioned. To _me_, the

deckmaster's creation) - as you must well know if you've been around for as

monitored and posted in the appropriate group(s) that existed at any given

to specific concerns then you're getting into an area where you can't be
guaranteed satisfaction. Why do I suspect that the process you described
has not inevitably led to the kind of results you claim? Tell me - did anyone
object to the Convocation's directive on card sleeves on the mailing lists?

long as) Jyhad's existed. This board has only been around for 5 months as
things stand. So perhaps you'll get some satisfaction on some of these things,
yet.

>Why do you have a problem in understanding that most of the people here
>only want to see a similar level of feedback/response for WotC's other game?

All right - that's a fair enough comment to make. I'm surprised to find
a perception that there's a lot of difference between how the two games are
treated by WotC. I'm certainly learning about that perception very fast.

Fred

pretty much as detailed and verbose as ever they were, near as I can tell.

references which I haven't read. I still claim there are clearly arbitrary
decisions that have been made and furthermore arbritrary decisions with more
game implications than the "red" vs. "orange" issue I raised above. To go
back to Magic (since there's no literary references to worry about, there),
a better example would be, "Why did they make exactly one flying, non-tap-to
attack 4/4 creature and give it to white?". The Serra Angel certainly has
incredible game implications and I'll bet anything they never really planned
it. Maybe it started as a 3/3 and they decided to bump it up in playtest or
maybe it started as a 5/5 and they cut it back - but I'll bet almost all of
the original cards (and many of the expansion cards) - were created totally
arbitrarily, without thought to implications they would have. Playtesting
may well have altered many of them on the way out the door and some others
were undoubtably "purpose" cards with very tangible reasons behind them.
But my point is that not every question "why" in game design has a profound
answer. This seems obvious to me.

different people have different opinions on the value of ancedotal evidence
and I've indicated before that I certainly think WotC should consider it.
But even if they do 1) there's no indication whatsoever of what degree of
confidence they can have that the results are representative of the general
population and 2) I still say popular will is often not a good basis for
designing (or REdesigning) a game. For instance, everyone may agree there's
a problem but any possible solution you can think up might create a worse
problem - not all problems with games are solvable in a satisfactory way.
(Diplomacy is a great example of a game with numerous problems that can't
really be solved.)

want us to know it. I don't really see any room for improvement as far as
communication goes. If the games itself isn't what you think is best, that
might be because the DT isn't as good as we could hope they'd be or it can
also mean that they have different tastes in how the game should play. I
guess you can interpret it how you like.

That's just it, I don't think they are. I think that whether you define
something in a game as a "problem" or not usually depends on your subjective
opinion of what is constitutes a problem. Now, some people's tastes in games
are quite a bit more refined than others - just as some people's tastes in
art or wine or whatever can be discernably superior to others - but in the
end, there's no objective statement to be made when consensus in this newsgroup
differs from (what is apparently) consensus on the DT.

It is not what I'm saying. I am saying that any average Joe can express an
opinion about how I should do my job. But unless Joe has to DO my job -
and not just a job LIKE my job at another company but MY JOB PERIOD, with
my boss in my environment dealing with the details I have to deal with -
then he doesn't necessarily know what the hell he's talking about. He
MIGHT be able to make a good suggestion every now and again but at the same
time he might be way fuckin' out to lunch because of some detail or daily
practicality of which he can have no clue (and not to blame him, he just
doesn't know).

And what is true of my job, I feel, is also likely to be true of the design
team members' jobs. THAT'S what I'm saying.

Fred

I have had a great deal of experience of that sort with reasonable and
sensible posters as well. I have also had a great deal of experience to the

superior choices for the membership of the DT than who's on it now. I

Deciding whether the losing gladiator lived or died was probably a lot of fun
for the crowds at the Coliseum but it was no system of justice.
